issues.legal_issue: A lease is not vitiated by fraud when the evidence does not establish fraud or misrepresentation in obtaining it.
material_facts: The lease was granted on the representation that the land was required for cooperative cultivation, although no cooperative society had been formed.

The Collector’s offer contained conditions consistent with the Collector knowing that no cooperative society existed, and an official endorsement recorded that the land was given for cultivation on a cooperative basis.
Neither the landholder nor his personal guardian testified to support the allegation of fraud.
issues.conclusion: The lease was not vitiated by fraud; the allegation of fraud, misrepresentation, or conspiracy was not established.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the evidence established the alleged fraud and found that it did not. No provision or earlier case was relied on to resolve this evidentiary issue.

predicates.lease_obtained_for_stated_cooperative_us: The authority granted a lease after being told that the land was required for cooperative use.
predicates.official_record_indicates_authority_knew: The official record contained terms or endorsements indicating that the authority knew no cooperative society existed.
predicates.landholder_side_did_not_testify_to_suppo: The landholder and the person responsible for protecting his interests did not testify to support the allegation of fraud.

issues.definition: When a lease is granted for stated cooperative use and the official record indicates the authority knew no society existed, or the landholder’s side does not testify to support the fraud claim, the lease is not proved to be fraudulent.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant does not acquire statutory ownership through a general acquisition date or the release of managed land when the relevant tenancy provisions do not apply at the acquisition date and no qualifying tenancy subsists when management ends.
material_facts: The land was under management of the Court of Wards when the tenancy provisions were amended to exclude land under that management from the relevant provisions.
The lease was created after that exclusion took effect and provided for expiry before management of the land ended.
The Court found that the tenancy provisions did not apply to the land during the period of management and that no tenancy subsisted when management ended.
issues.conclusion: The defendants did not become statutory owners under section 32 or the first proviso to section 88.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, a qualifying tenant could acquire the land on the tillers’ day. Section 88(1), as amended, made sections 1 to 87A inapplicable to land under Court of Wards management, while its first proviso applied the provisions after release and provided a purchase right for a tenancy subsisting on release. Because the tenancy provisions did not apply during management and no tenancy subsisted at release, neither route gave the defendants statutory ownership.

rule.if: claim_for_statutory_land_ownership and land_under_protected_management and tenancy_provisions_unavailable_on_general_acquisition_date and not qualifying_tenancy_on_general_acquisition_date and not tenancy_subsisting_when_management_ended

predicates.claim_for_statutory_land_ownership: A party claimed ownership of land by relying on statutory tenancy rights.
predicates.land_under_protected_management: The land was under a form of management that excluded it from the relevant tenancy provisions.
predicates.tenancy_provisions_unavailable_on_genera: The tenancy provisions providing for statutory acquisition did not apply to the land on the general acquisition date.
predicates.qualifying_tenancy_on_general_acquisitio: The claimant held a tenancy that qualified for statutory acquisition on the general acquisition date.
predicates.tenancy_subsisting_when_management_ended: A tenancy subsisted in the land when the protected management ended.

issues.definition: A claim to statutory ownership fails when the land was under protected management, the relevant tenancy provisions were unavailable on the general acquisition date, and no qualifying tenancy existed on that date or subsisted when management ended.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court may decide whether statutory ownership was acquired and whether a party was a tenant on past dates when the past tenancy is raised as the basis for the ownership claim.
material_facts: The defendants claimed statutory ownership based on alleged tenancy on past dates, rather than asserting an independent current-tenancy issue as the basis of that claim.
Deciding the ownership claim required deciding whether the tenancy provisions applied to the land during the relevant period.

The statutory duty assigned to the revenue authority concerned whether a person is a tenant, and the Court construed it as not requiring that authority to decide whether the person had been a tenant in the past.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction was not barred from deciding whether statutory ownership had been acquired, including the subsidiary questions of past tenancy and whether the Act applied to the land during a particular period.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 70(b) and 85 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act did not exclude civil jurisdiction over the title claim or its subsidiary questions about past tenancy and the Act’s applicability. Section 70(b) imposed a duty to decide whether a person is a tenant, not whether the person was a tenant in the past. The Court applied the principle in Secretary of State v. Mask & Co., 67 I.A. 222, 236, that exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred and must be express or clearly implied.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_claim_to_statutory_t: A civil suit includes a claim that a party acquired ownership under a statutory land-tenancy scheme.
predicates.past_tenancy_is_subsidiary_to_title_clai: The alleged tenancy on past dates is advanced as support for the ownership claim rather than as an independent current-tenancy claim.

issues.definition: When a civil suit involves a statutory title claim and past tenancy is only subsidiary to that claim, the civil court may decide the title claim and the past-tenancy issue.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court should not refer a tenancy issue to the revenue authority when no independent issue of tenancy on the suit date survives for decision.
material_facts: The defendants’ pleaded tenancy claim was based on an alleged lease created before the tenancy provisions ceased to apply to the managed land and was used to support their statutory-ownership claim.
The lease expired before management ended, and the defendants did not plead an intervening transaction creating a new tenancy that subsisted on the suit date.
The High Court referred the question whether the defendants were tenants of the land to the revenue authority.
issues.conclusion: There was no issue surviving for referral to the Mamlatdar; the High Court should have decided the suit and restored the trial court’s decree for possession, damages, and mesne profits.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 85A of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, a civil court refers issues that are required to be decided by a competent authority under the Act. Section 70(b) assigns the Mamlatdar the duty to decide whether a person is a tenant, not whether that person was a tenant in the past. With no independent pleaded claim of tenancy subsisting on the suit date, no issue remained for referral.

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A civil suit seeks possession of land from a party occupying it.
predicates.tenancy_defence_rests_only_on_past_lease: The defence relies only on an earlier lease, including as the basis for a statutory-ownership claim.
predicates.no_new_tenancy_pleaded_for_suit_date: The party asserting tenancy did not plead a later transaction creating a tenancy that subsisted on the suit date.

issues.definition: When a possession suit is defended only by reliance on a past lease and no new tenancy is pleaded for the suit date, the civil court must decide the suit without referring a tenancy issue.
